pages.d: Get started with Material Web 3.0 and find the project information: quick start, migration, support, roadmap and browser support.
x: Getting started and project information: how to install and use Material Web 3.0, how it follows the Material 3 spec, what is coming next, and where to get help. Introduction: Material web, also known as Material Web Components or MWC, is a library of web components that follows Google's Material Design guidelines. Spec compliance: What the spec checks, ARIA and axe results, Baseline use and size budgets say about md-gb-* components. Quick Start: For fast prototyping, use a CDN such as esm.run to load @material/web without installing it. Migration: Version 3.0 renames most elements from md- to md-gb- and moves them to Material 3 Expressive. Roadmap: This roadmap describes current, future, and past goals for Material Web Components. Support: Version 3.0 targets Baseline widely available: the web platform features it uses have worked in all major browsers for at least 30 months. Bundle Sizes: Every md-gb- component is checked against a Brotli-compressed size budget for its JavaScript and CSS (the measured size plus 10% headroom), defined in scripts/size/gb-budgets.json. Browser support: Version 3.0 only uses web platform features that are Baseline widely available. AI agents: labs/gb/skill/ is a Claude Code skill named md-gb. Debugging: The shared plumbing of the components (motion waits, overflow measure passes, and scroll steps) can record performance marks. Use with shadcn/ui: Install the md-gb elements as React components with the shadcn CLI, themed by your shadcn variables.

pages.d: The principles Material Web 3.0 applies across its components: theming, interaction states, accessibility, adaptive layout and density.
x: The principles applied across every component: how theming works, how elements respond to input, and how they stay accessible and adapt to the space they get. Theming: Material Design theming creates unique branded products with familiar patterns and accessible interactions. Interaction States: Interactive components show their state with a state layer: a translucent overlay of the component's content color, drawn between the container and the content. Accessibility: Every labs/gb component works with a keyboard, a screen reader and reduced motion. Adaptive layout: Pages and components change with the window. Density: Density lets people see more information in data-heavy views by making components more compact. Layout: Layout adapts an app to the window with window size classes, a column grid, margins and panes. Scaffold: A scaffold arranges the bars, rails and panes around an app's content, and adapts them to the window size.

pages.d: The visual language of Material Web 3.0: color, typography, shape, elevation, icons, motion and spacing, as tokens you can use.
x: The visual language of Material 3 Expressive as tokens you can use: color, type, shape, elevation, icons, motion and spacing. Color: Color creates meaning and communicates hierarchy, state, and brand. Dynamic color: Dynamic color builds a full color scheme, light and dark, from a seed color. Typography: Typography helps make writing legible and beautiful. Shape: Shape can direct attention, communicate state, and express brand. Elevation: Elevation is the distance between two surfaces on the z-axis. Icons: md-gb-icon shows a Material Symbols icon. Material Symbols: md-gb-icon axes: optical size, weight, fill and grade. Motion: Motion makes a UI expressive and easy to follow: springs for physics, easing and duration tokens, and transition patterns. Transitions: Transition patterns connect elements and views, and skeleton loaders hold space while content loads. Spacing: Spacing is the distance around and between elements.

pages.d: Every md-gb element of Material Web 3.0: buttons, pickers, progress indicators, navigation, sheets and more, each with live examples and API.
x: The md-gb elements: interactive building blocks for your interface, each with live examples, guidelines and its API.

Button Group: A button group arranges related buttons and can manage their selection, density and overflow. Buttons: Buttons help people initiate actions, from sending an email, to sharing a document, to liking a post. FAB menu: A FAB menu opens from a FAB to show several related actions, and the FAB becomes its close button. Floating action button (FAB): A FAB represents the most important action on a screen, and an extended FAB adds a text label. Icon Buttons: Icon buttons help people take supplementary actions with a single tap. Segmented button: A segmented button set lets people pick one or several options from two to five segments, such as a time range or a view. Split button: A split button pairs a main action with a trailing button that opens a menu of related actions.
Date picker: A date picker lets people select a date or a range of dates. Time picker: Time pickers let people choose an hour and minute on a clock dial, or type them into fields.

Loading indicator: A loading indicator shows that a short process is running, with a shape that morphs through Material shapes while it turns. Progress indicators: Progress indicators inform people about the status of ongoing processes, such as loading an app or submitting a form. Pull to refresh: A pull to refresh container lets people pull its content down to reload it, with a loading indicator that shows progress.

Navigation Bar: A navigation bar lets people switch between a small number of top-level destinations, and can hide as the page scrolls. Navigation Drawer: A Material Design navigation drawer. Navigation Rail: A navigation rail lets people switch between top-level destinations on larger windows, and expands to show full labels.
Sheets: Sheets show supplementary content and actions anchored to the bottom or the side of the window.

App Bar: An app bar sits at the top of a screen and shows its title, navigation and actions, and can hide or compress as the page scrolls. Badge: A badge shows a small dot or a count to signal new or changed information. Card: A card contains content and actions about a single subject. Carousel: A carousel is a scrollable list of visual items that change size as they move through the layout. Checkbox: Checkboxes let people select one or more items from a set, or turn an option on or off. Chips: Chips help people enter information, make selections, filter content, or trigger actions. Dialogs: Dialogs provide important prompts in a user flow. Divider: A divider is a thin line that groups content in lists and containers. Lists: Lists are continuous, vertical indexes of text and images, with optional selection, reordering, expanding and swipe actions. Menus: Menus show a temporary set of actions or choices, opened from a button, a text field or a context. Radio: Radio buttons let people select one option from a set of options. Search: A search bar lets people enter a query and find matching results, with a search view that shows suggestions and results. Select: Select menus let people choose one option from a list that opens on a temporary surface. Sliders: Sliders let people view and select a value, or a range of values, along a track. Snackbar: Snackbars tell people about a process an app has performed or will perform, without interrupting them. Switch: Switches toggle the state of an item on or off. Tabs: Tabs organize groups of related content that are at the same level of hierarchy. Text field: Text fields let people enter and edit text. Toolbar: A toolbar holds actions that relate to the content on the screen, docked to an edge or floating above it. Tooltip: Tooltips add context to a button or other element, as a short plain label or a richer panel with a subhead and actions.

pages.d: Material web, also known as Material Web Components or MWC, is a library of web components that follows Google's Material Design guidelines.
x: Material Design is a design system built and supported by Google designers and developers. Guidelines for building Material apps and components are published on material.io. Version 3.0 implements Material 3 Expressive, the latest evolution of Material 3: a larger shape scale with shape morphing, spring-based motion, an emphasized type scale, and an updated dynamic color system. The elements are named md-gb-*, follow the WAI-ARIA patterns for their roles, and only rely on web platform features that are Baseline widely available (newer features are guarded and degrade gracefully).

Web components are custom HTML elements with encapsulated styles and behavior. They work across many different frameworks (such as Lit, React, Vue, and Svelte) as well as web environments (such as Eleventy, Wordpress, and Ruby on Rails). Many components in this library are drop-in replacements for browser elements like <button> and <input>. Every element is prefixed with md-gb-. Example: A form with a text field and a button

Design tokens are the building blocks of all UI elements. Here they are CSS custom properties that you can override to style components. Version 3.0 provides the system tokens for color, typography, shape, elevation, space, and motion. Example: A button with an olive primary color HTML CSS

pages.d: A button group arranges related buttons and can manage their selection, density and overflow.
x: Example: A standard button group of three buttons

Choose standard or connected. In a standard group, buttons respond to the one that is pressed; a connected group joins them into one control. Keep buttons alike. Use the same size and shape for every button, and mix sizes only for hero moments. Group related buttons. Mix colors and widths to emphasize what matters and to group related actions. Let it adapt. On narrow screens, trailing buttons can collapse into an overflow menu. This component is new in M3 Expressive.
A button group holds md-gb-button elements, each with an optional icon. Example: A button group of three buttons with an icon and a label
Set variant="connected" for buttons that sit together as a single control. Example: A connected button group

Set selection to single or multiple and give each button a value. Add required to keep one selected in a single-select group. A group fires input and change when selection changes. Example: A single-select button group with Week selected
Buttons in a group can be icon-only. Give each one an aria-label. Example: A button group of icon buttons
Set density from 0 (default) to -3 to make the buttons shorter. Touch targets stay 48px. Example: A button group with density -2

Add overflow-menu to collapse the buttons that don't fit into a menu at the trailing edge. Choosing a menu entry clicks the original button. Example: A button group with an overflow menu in a narrow container

The group does not need a label of its own, but a name such as aria-label="Text alignment" helps when the buttons form a set. Label each button as you would a button; icon-only buttons need aria-label. Tab enters the group, Arrow keys move between buttons, and Enter or Space activates the focused button.

pages.d: Material Design theming creates unique branded products with familiar patterns and accessible interactions.
x: Material is expressed in design tokens, which are the building blocks of all UI elements. In 3.0, the md-gb-* elements are themed with system tokens, which map roles to concrete reference values. Load them once for the document with adoptStyles(), then override any token with CSS. Example: Load the system tokens once for the document HTML JavaScript System tokens are CSS custom properties in the md.sys.* cascade layers, so unlayered CSS always wins and they can be scoped with any selector. Example: A scope where buttons have square corners HTML CSS

System tokens define the decisions and roles that give the design system its character: color, typography, shape, elevation, space, and motion. Color --md-sys-color tokens define the dynamic color roles. They use light-dark(), so they follow color-scheme. See the color guide. Example: A button with a custom primary color for light and dark HTML CSS Typography --md-sys-typescale tokens define the type scale, including the emphasized styles. See the typography guide. Example: Body text with a larger size and line height HTML CSS Shape --md-sys-shape tokens define the corner scale, including single-corner values. See the shape guide. Example: A box with custom medium and large corners HTML CSS Motion --md-sys-motion tokens define the motion scheme: spring tokens (--md-sys-motion-spring-<speed>-<spatial|effects>, each with a matching -duration), easing curves, and durations. Springs are linear() easings. The standard scheme applies to elements inside .md-motion-standard. Example: A panel that slides with the default spatial spring HTML CSS JavaScript

pages.d: Color creates meaning and communicates hierarchy, state, and brand.
x: The page follows the subpages of the M3 color guidance in order. All imports come from @material/web/labs/gb/styles/color/.

The system turns a few inputs into a complete, accessible set of colors. Dynamic color starts from a source color, runs it through a scheme algorithm, derives five key colors (primary, secondary, tertiary, neutral, neutral variant) plus error, builds a tonal palette for each in HCT (hue, chroma, tone), and assigns tones to color roles. Roles come with a pairing rule: a color and its on- color are chosen so text and icons stay legible. Each role has three contrast levels (standard, medium, high), so the same scheme can serve people who need more contrast. In labs/gb: md-color-tokens.css is the static baseline: every role as a --md-sys-color-<role> custom property, with light and dark values. md-color-tokens-contrast.css adds medium and high contrast. High contrast follows prefers-contrast: more, and .md-contrast-standard, .md-contrast-medium and .md-contrast-high select a level for a subtree. md-color-tokens-full.css also declares the reference palette (--md-ref-palette-*), the tonal palettes the roles are picked from. dynamic-color.ts runs the generation steps at runtime with Material Color Utilities (see Dynamic color below). The new tone-based surface roles (container levels, dim, and bright) and the fixed accent roles from the latest spec are all part of the tokens, so nothing extra is needed to use them. HCT is also available as a small API (see Advanced customization).

A role is a named job for a color, not a specific hue. Components read roles (primary, surface-container) instead of hex values, so a new scheme re-themes everything. The spec groups them as accent roles (primary, secondary, tertiary, error, each with on-, -container and on-container variants), surface roles with on-surface and on-surface-variant, outline roles, inverse roles, and add-on roles: fixed accents and bright and dim surfaces. Layer from lower to higher emphasis, and always put on- content on its matching background. Use surface-dim and surface-bright for areas that stay darker or brighter than the main surface in both themes. Example: A card and a badge colored with roles HTML CSS

The tokens use light-dark(), so they follow the standard color-scheme property. Where light-dark() is not available, the Baseline fallback keeps the light values and switches to the dark values with prefers-color-scheme. Example: Two boxes: one follows the system color scheme, one is always dark HTML CSS The deprecated background and surface-tint roles are not defined; use surface and a surface container instead.

Pick static color when you want a fixed, predictable palette: a brand identity, a product with a strict visual identity, or a small, controlled UI. Pick dynamic color when the palette should come from the person or the content: a wallpaper, a profile color, an album cover. You can also mix both: a dynamic scheme for most of the UI and static colors for brand and semantic meaning. In labs/gb that is a choice of which stylesheet or function you load: Static: import md-color-tokens.css (and md-color-tokens-contrast.css if you want contrast levels). No JavaScript. Dynamic: call themeFromSource(), themeFromImage() or applyTheme(), which output the same custom properties and override the static ones.

The spec has two kinds. Baseline is the default purple scheme, ready to use and a good starting point for prototypes. Custom brand keeps the same roles but replaces the key colors with your brand colors, usually exported from the Material Theme Builder or a design tool. Baseline in labs/gb is the default stylesheet. It is also part of m3Styles, which adoptStyles() loads. Example: A sample colored with the baseline tokens HTML CSS For a custom brand scheme, override the tokens by hand, or generate the roles once and keep the CSS. Example: A button in a custom teal brand color HTML CSS Example: A button themed with CSS generated from a source color HTML TypeScript To start from a Material Theme Builder export, pass its JSON to themeFromThemeBuilder(), or apply it live with themeOptionsFromThemeBuilder(). Example: A button themed with a Material Theme Builder export HTML TypeScript The seed (or the core primary) is the source, other core colors become palettes, extended colors become harmonized or exact customColors, and a variant or contrast field in the file is used if present. The generated schemes and palettes in the export are ignored, so the roles match the rest of labs/gb. A second argument overrides any option.

A dynamic scheme is generated from a source. The spec distinguishes user-generated color (a wallpaper or a person's pick, usually with the tonal-spot variant), content-based color (taken from an image or content on screen, with the content variant), and multiple sources (several schemes on one screen, each scoped to a region). Example: A button themed at runtime with medium contrast HTML TypeScript For content-based color, scope the scheme to one element with a source taken from an image: Example: A card themed from the color of its image HTML CSS TypeScript To get the theme without applying it, use themeFromSource() or themeFromImage(img), and themeToStyleSheet(theme) for a stylesheet. Variants: tonal-spot, neutral, vibrant, expressive, fidelity, content, monochrome, rainbow, and fruit-salad. The spec page does not define these variants or any version of their rules; they come from Material Color Utilities, which has 2025 rules only for tonal spot, neutral, vibrant and expressive. The others use the original rules, so labs/gb does too. theme.specVersion reports what was used. Contrast: standard, medium, high, or a number from -1 to 1. applyTheme() accepts contrast: 'auto', which uses high contrast when the user prefers more contrast. Platform: phone (also right for the web) or watch. applyTheme(target, ...) accepts a document, a shadow root, or an element. An element gets inline custom properties, so its subtree has its own scheme. clearTheme() removes it. Android's system-wide wallpaper source and the Material Theme Builder preview are not part of labs/gb; the library only generates the scheme. When using content-based color, keep semantic colors (error, success) stable and make sure the surrounding UI stays readable if the image is very saturated or very dark. The scheme already guarantees accessible on-color pairs.

The spec lists three kinds of customization. This table shows what labs/gb covers. Spec topic In labs/gb Combine multiple color schemes Yes: call applyTheme(element, ...) on different elements, each with its own source, variant and contrast. Map or remap colors on UI elements Yes: components read roles, so reassign a role in CSS (--md-sys-color-surface: var(--md-sys-color-surface-container);) on a subtree. Define static colors Yes: customColors adds a color with four roles. Define custom color roles Yes: customRoles takes a name, a palette and a tone for light and dark (optionally per contrast level). Define your own baseline scheme Yes: override the static tokens, or pass palettes. Define your own dynamic scheme Yes: palettes takes your own primary, secondary, tertiary, neutral, neutral variant and error key colors. Use color fidelity Yes: fidelity per role. Harmonize colors Yes: customColors harmonize toward the source by default, and harmonize(color, source) is exported. Example: Swatches of a harmonized and an exact custom color HTML CSS TypeScript Harmonize colors that carry meaning but should still sit in the theme, such as success and warning. Do not harmonize brand colors that must stay exact.

A custom role is one color picked from a palette at a reference tone, for light and dark, so it follows the source color and the contrast level like the built-in roles. It makes --md-sys-color-<name> only; pick a tone that meets contrast against the role it sits on (3:1 for graphics) and check the pair yourself. Example: Swatches of two custom color roles HTML CSS TypeScript palette is one of primary, secondary, tertiary, neutral, neutralVariant, error. Tones are 0 to 100; a number applies to both themes.

Colors in the system are built in HCT (hue, chroma, tone). To work in it yourself: Example: Colors computed in HCT HTML TypeScript Colors outside the sRGB range are brought in by lowering chroma. Prefer an existing role before adding custom colors, and keep contrast pairs accessible; customColors roles follow the same on-color convention as the accents.

node scripts/m3/audit-gb.mjs --gaps compares every token declaration in the labs/gb token files with the M3 token database. Label the action. A button's text describes what happens when it is pressed, such as "Save" or "Join now". Match emphasis to importance. Use filled for the final action of a flow, tonal and outlined for medium emphasis, and text for the lowest priority. Use elevated sparingly. Elevated buttons add a shadow, so reserve them for buttons that need separation from a patterned background. Add an icon to draw attention. An icon can help communicate the action.
A button is one element holding a label and an optional icon (default slot). It renders a native <button> or, with href, a link. Example: A filled button with an icon and a label

pages.d: Interactive components show their state with a state layer: a translucent overlay of the component's content color, drawn between the container and the content.
x: Interactive components show their state with a state layer: a translucent overlay of the component's content color, drawn between the container and the content. Components handle this for you. You only need to know which state shows which layer. State Layer opacity When Hover 8% A cursor rests over the element (hover-capable input) Focus 10% Keyboard or voice focus Pressed 10% A tap or click is in progress Dragged 16% The element is being dragged Hover and focus combine. A focused, hovered element shows the focus layer too. Disabled components show no state layers: they cannot be focused, dragged or pressed, and they do not inherit hover.
Hover only where it is real

Hover applies only on devices that can hover, through @media (hover: hover). A tap on a touch screen does not leave the hover layer on. Do not hide essential content or controls behind hover, because touch users never see it.

The pressed state plays a ripple, with this timing: The layer fades in over 75ms. The circle grows over 225ms (fast-out, slow-in), while its center moves to the middle. Once the press is released and the growth is done, the layer fades out over 150ms. A quick tap still shows the ripple for at least 225ms, so a press always reads as a press. Use the ripple as written. Do not add a second press effect on top of it.
Components apply their states on their own. Use them like any other element. Example: A button and an icon button, both with state layers

Do not restyle the state layer colors per screen. The opacities are part of the state, so keep them as they are. Do not tell people to "hover to see" an action. Show it, or give it a visible label. Keep focus visible. The focus layer is not a replacement for the focus ring.

pages.d: Every labs/gb component works with a keyboard, a screen reader and reduced motion.
x: The rules below are the ones the components follow and the tests check.

Composite components (button groups, chip sets, lists, menus, tabs, navigation, pickers) share one roving focus model in labs/gb/components/shared/roving-focus.ts: Arrow keys move between items along the orientation. Left and Right follow the reading direction, so they mirror in RTL. Home and End go to the first and last item. Focus wraps at the ends unless the component turns wrapping off. Disabled items are skipped. Soft-disabled items stay focusable. Only one item is in the tab order at a time (roving tabindex). Tab enters the group on the item that was focused last, or the first one. Keys pressed with Alt, Ctrl, Meta or Shift are left to the browser. Escape clears keyboard focus: it hides the focus indicator and starts the focus order over, so Tab after Escape reaches the first focusable element again. In a text field, Escape removes the cursor and keeps the typed text. If a handler already used the Escape key, the component leaves it alone. A dialog fires cancel on Escape, a scrim click or the full-screen close button. Canceling keeps the dialog open if you call preventDefault(): Example: A dialog that stays open on Escape while there are unsaved changes HTML JavaScript

The focus ring is drawn with outline, using the --focus-ring-outline and --focus-ring-offset variables from labs/gb/components/focus/focus-ring.scss. The thickness, color and offsets come from the state focus indicator tokens, so a theme changes them in one place. Do not remove the outline with CSS unless you draw a replacement that passes the same tests.

Components use WAI-ARIA 1.3 roles, states and properties. The model of the draft and the checks that report misuse live in labs/gb/components/shared/central/aria_test.ts. Axe-core runs against every component in labs/gb/components/shared/central/axe_test.ts, so a missing label or an invalid attribute fails the suite. Material Design 3 wins where it and WAI-ARIA 1.3 disagree. In every other case the ARIA rules apply as written. When you add a component, follow the M3 page for its behavior first, then check the ARIA role and attributes it uses.

Motion respects prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. The motion helpers in labs/gb/components/shared/motion.ts resolve to 0 ms under that setting and inside an ancestor with the md-motion-reduced class. The motion tokens in labs/gb/styles/motion/ follow the same rule. Ripples skip the animated press and show their end state, and the effect tokens (color, opacity, shape) do not change. Do not animate with hard-coded durations. Read the duration from the motion helpers or the tokens, so reduced motion applies to your component too.

pages.d: Typography helps make writing legible and beautiful.
x: Tip: "typeface" and "typescale" can be confusing. "face" refers to font-family and font-weight. "scale" refers to a group of font-family, font-size, line-height, and font-weight tokens.

A typeface is a font-family. In Material there are plain and brand typefaces. Each typeface has normal, medium, and bold styles (defaults to 400, 500, and 700). All three weight styles need to be included for a font. Important: the default typeface is Roboto Flex, then Roboto. If you do not change it, load one of them. For example, from fonts.google.com.

Typefaces can be set using CSS custom properties. Tokens follow the naming convention --md-ref-typeface-<token>. Typeface Token Brand --md-ref-typeface-brand Plain --md-ref-typeface-plain All tokens Example: A heading in the brand typeface and text in the plain typeface HTML CSS

A typescale is a collection of font styles: font-family, font-size, line-height, and font-weight. They are organized into roles that describe their purpose. Material's applying type guidelines explains when to use each typescale role.
The type scale is applied with the font shorthand tokens and their -axes and -tracking companions, which also work inside shadow roots. Example: A heading in the medium display style HTML CSS

The scale has five roles (display, headline, title, body, label), each in sm, md, and lg, plus emphasized styles per role. Tokens follow --md-sys-typescale-<role>-<size>-<property> with the properties font, size, line-height, weight, tracking, and axes; the bare --md-sys-typescale-<role>-<size> is the combined font shorthand. Typescale Tokens Display --md-sys-typescale-display-md-size, -line-height, -weight Headline --md-sys-typescale-headline-md-size, -line-height, -weight Title --md-sys-typescale-title-md-size, -line-height, -weight Body --md-sys-typescale-body-md-size, -line-height, -weight Label --md-sys-typescale-label-md-size, -line-height, -weight Emphasized --md-sys-typescale-emphasized-<role>-<size> Language height. Line heights adapt to the script. Set --md-sys-language-height-scale (1, 1.07, 1.3, or 2) on :root to change the default; text in languages such as Arabic, Thai, or Urdu picks up its height from :lang(). pages.d: Icon buttons help people take supplementary actions with a single tap.

Use a clear icon. Pick a system icon whose meaning people already know, and give the button an accessible name that describes the action. Describe the action on hover. On the web, add a tooltip so the action is named while hovering or focusing the button. Pick the color by emphasis. Filled is the most prominent, tonal and outlined are medium, and the standard color suits the lowest priority. Show state with a toggle. A toggle button uses the outlined icon when unselected and the filled icon when selected.
An icon button is one element that holds an icon (default slot). It renders a native <button> or, with href, a link. Example: A filled icon button with a send icon

pages.d: Density lets people see more information in data-heavy views by making components more compact.
x: Density lets people see more information in data-heavy views by making components more compact. A component's density is a number from 0 (the default) to -3 (the densest). Each step down makes the component smaller. Values are rounded and clamped to that range. Use the density attribute. Example: Checkboxes at density 0 and -3

density is available on these components: md-gb-button-group md-gb-checkbox md-gb-chip md-gb-icon-button md-gb-list md-gb-menu md-gb-radio md-gb-segmented-button md-gb-switch md-gb-tabs md-gb-text-field md-gb-time-picker Each step shrinks the component's visual size, not its touch target. A checkbox, for example, loses 4px from its layout box (48px at density 0) and its state layer (40px at density 0) per step. Its touch target stays 48px.
md-gb-button-group md-gb-checkbox md-gb-chip md-gb-icon-button md-gb-list md-gb-menu md-gb-radio md-gb-segmented-button md-gb-switch md-gb-tabs md-gb-text-field md-gb-time-picker

Every component keeps a touch target of at least 48 by 48 CSS pixels, even at the densest setting. The visual element can be smaller, but the area that responds to a tap cannot. Do not override this with your own sizing.

Density is a choice, not a default. Leave components at 0 unless the view is data-heavy, and let people opt into a denser layout where you offer a control for it. Do not change density automatically. It should not switch when the window resizes or the device rotates, unless the person changed it. Consider the device. A person may want a dense desktop layout but not a dense phone layout. Layout density comes first. Spacing changes can add information without shrinking components. Use component density when you also need the controls themselves to be smaller. Keep the controls accessible. If you offer a density setting, the setting itself must be easy to find and use.

pages.d: Elevation is the distance between two surfaces on the z-axis.
x: Elevation is the distance between two surfaces on the z-axis. It tells people which surface sits in front, which one sits behind, and which one is the current focus. Every surface and component has an elevation, so keep the number of levels small.

There are six levels, 0 to 5. Each one has a token: --md-sys-elevation-shadow-0 (no shadow) to --md-sys-elevation-shadow-5 Levels 0 to 3 are for resting components. Levels 4 and 5 are for interaction states, such as hover and drag. Components raise by one level when hovered or focused: a FAB goes from level 3 to level 4, and a filled button goes from level 0 to level 1. The tokens are defined in labs/gb/styles/elevation/md-elevation-tokens.scss. Shadow colors come from --md-sys-color-shadow, so they adapt to the color scheme.

Each component has a fixed resting level. Do not change it on your own. Level Components 0 Buttons (filled, tonal, outlined), button group, split button, icon buttons, chips, segmented button, cards (filled, outlined), carousel, list, navigation rail, tabs, slider, app bar (not scrolled), full-screen dialog, docked side sheet 1 Elevated button, elevated card, elevated chip, modal navigation drawer, modal bottom sheet, modal side sheet 2 Menu, navigation bar, rich tooltip 3 FAB (small, standard and extended), FAB menu close button, modal dialog, date picker, time picker, floating toolbar, full-screen dialog above compact windows (where it is a basic dialog) The search bar also rests at level 0 without a shadow, but it shows its level by tone (see below).

Elevation can be shown with a tonal surface color instead of a shadow. Two components do this in gb: Search bar: no shadow. Its container uses surface-container-high, the tone for level 3. App bar when scrolled: no drop shadow. Its container changes from surface to surface-container, the tone for level 2, so it separates from the content under it. Use tone when a surface only needs to be told apart from what is behind it.

Shadows are for two cases only: to protect an element on a busy or patterned background, and to encourage interaction, such as a card that lifts on hover. Otherwise rely on the tonal difference between surfaces, which is the default. A small, sharp shadow means the surface is close to the one behind it. A larger, softer shadow means more distance.
Example: A note card that lifts from level 1 to level 2 on hover HTML CSS

Do not hard-code shadow values. Use the level tokens so a change to the scale reaches every surface. Avoid changing the default elevation of a component. When an interaction such as hover changes it, make the change the same for every similar component. Give floating elements enough contrast with the surface beneath them, either through the shadow or through a tone difference.

pages.d: Version 3.0 targets Baseline widely available: the web platform features it uses have worked in all major browsers for at least 30 months.

Newer features (such as corner-shape or light-dark()) are only used behind @supports guards or with a fallback, so components stay usable in older engines. The repository checks this with npm run gb:baseline. See Browser support for the minimum versions.
How do I change the color of a button?

Components read --md-sys-color-* tokens. Override the key color a component uses on the element or a class. Buttons use primary, and the states (hover, focus, pressed) are derived from it. Example: A button that uses the error colors HTML CSS
Why doesn't prefers-color-scheme: dark switch the theme?
The tokens use light-dark(), so they follow the color-scheme property. Set it to follow the system, or force a scheme on any subtree. Example: A subtree that is always dark HTML CSS
How do I generate my own --md-sys-color-* tokens?

Generate a theme from a source color at runtime, or export a stylesheet. Example: A button themed from a source color HTML JavaScript You can also design a scheme with the Material Theme Builder Figma plugin. See Color.
How do I style an element inside another component?
Use CSS ::part(). The parts of each component are listed under its CSS parts in the API reference.

pages.d: md-gb-icon shows a Material Symbols icon.
x: md-gb-icon shows a Material Symbols icon. Its content is the ligature name of the symbol, such as home. Find names and previews at fonts.google.com/icons. Symbols come in three styles: outlined, rounded and sharp. The element is a thin wrapper over the font. It reads its size, color and font variation settings from custom properties.

The element's default font family is Material Symbols. The Google Fonts family for the outlined style is Material Symbols Outlined, so set --md-icon-font to the family you load: Example: An icon in the outlined Material Symbols family HTML CSS Load the font once in the page head. Request only the axes you use; add GRAD to use --md-icon-grad. Example: An icon with the font loaded by a link tag

--md-icon-size sets the size. The default is 24px. Symbols support 20dp, 24dp, 40dp and 48dp; use 20dp for dense layouts and 40dp or 48dp for display use. --md-icon-color sets the color. The default is currentColor. The optical size follows the icon size automatically, so a larger icon gets a matching optical size. Set --md-icon-opsz only to override it.

Each style has four axes. The element exposes them as custom properties: Property Axis Default Range Notes --md-icon-wght Weight 400 100 to 700 400 is the 2dp stroke for standard icons. Use at least 200 at 24dp. --md-icon-fill Fill 0 0 to 1 1 is filled, 0 is outlined. The change animates. --md-icon-grad Grade 0 Negative to positive Gb sets -25 when the color scheme is dark, where icons are light on dark. Positive values add emphasis. --md-icon-opsz Optical size follows size 20 to 48dp Not set by default. Fill is the usual way to show a selected state. Use the outlined symbol when the item is unselected and the filled one when it is selected.

Symbols next to text need a baseline shift to line up. The element already applies vertical-align: -0.115em (of its own size), which lowers the icon so it lines up with the text beside it: about 2.8px at 24dp. Keep that vertical-align if you override the style, or the icon will look too high.

A 24dp icon needs a 48dp target by default. A 20dp icon can use a 40dp target when a mouse and keyboard are the main input. md-gb-icon-button keeps a 48dp minimum target (--target-size) even when the icon inside is smaller, so use it rather than a bare icon in a clickable element.

An icon is decorative unless it has a label. md-gb-icon sets aria-hidden="true" by default, so screen readers skip it. That is correct when the text beside the icon already says what it means. For an icon-only control, put the accessible name on the control with aria-label, and leave the icon hidden. Only set aria-hidden="false" on an icon that must be announced on its own. Add a text label when the symbol is abstract, complex, or carries a key action. A symbol shown below 20dp should have one too.

Change an axis or the size with the custom properties. Example: A default icon, a filled icon and a large bold icon Put the accessible name on the control, not on the icon. Example: An icon-only button with an accessible name

An icon with no font loaded shows the ligature text, such as favorite, not a symbol. Load the font before the page relies on it. Do not mix styles in one icon set. Pick outlined, rounded or sharp for the whole product. Do not use the lightest weight for standard 24dp icons. Keep the icon's content inside the 20dp live area of the 24dp grid. It can reach into the 2dp padding for extra weight, but never past the 24dp edge.

Newer features are either guarded with @supports or allowed to be ignored where a browser lacks them. The exceptions are listed, with the reason for each, in scripts/gb-baseline-allow.json. pages.d: Motion makes a UI expressive and easy to follow: springs for physics, easing and duration tokens, and transition patterns.
x: Material 3 Expressive uses a physics-based motion system. Springs drive spatial motion (position, size, rotation, corner shape) and effects springs drive properties that must not overshoot, like color and opacity. One spring can serve transitions, button effects and gestures, which keeps the product feeling consistent. Each spring is exposed as a CSS linear() easing with a matching duration, so a transition can use it directly.

Expressive is the default. Use it for most situations, especially hero moments and key interactions. Spatial springs overshoot and bounce into place. Standard moves with minimal bounce and suits utilitarian products. Apply it to a subtree with the md-motion-standard class. The spec's three levels of customization map to CSS like this: Use a default scheme: do nothing (Expressive), or add md-motion-standard. Create a custom scheme: override the spring custom properties in your own :root rule. Swap the scheme for one element: put md-motion-standard on that element. Example: A button in a subtree that uses the standard motion scheme

Spring tokens follow --md-sys-motion-spring-<speed>-<spatial|effects>, with fast, default and slow speeds. Each has a -duration token: Example: A panel that slides with the default spatial spring HTML CSS JavaScript Spring Expressive Standard Spatial fast / default / slow 350 / 420 / 570ms 160 / 220 / 340ms Effects fast / default / slow 140 / 220 / 300ms 140 / 220 / 300ms Springs handle interruption and retargeting well, so prefer them. For animations without interruptions or gestures you can use the curve fallback: --md-sys-motion-curve-<speed>-<spatial|effects> (a cubic-bezier()) with --md-sys-motion-curve-<speed>-<spatial|effects>-duration. They carry the values from the spec's web conversion table.

Reduced motion is on when the platform asks for it (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) or inside an element with the md-motion-reduced class (spatial motion is off there, fades stay). The spatial springs then become instant (0ms) and the effects springs keep their timing. People still see fades and color changes, but not sliding, scaling, parallax or shape morphing. Do not build your own motion gate. Read the durations from the tokens so the scheme and reduced motion apply without extra code.

A gesture has to keep its momentum: a fling that lets go at 2000px/s must not restart from rest, and a settle that is aimed at a new target half way must not jump. A CSS transition cannot do either, so labs/gb also has the same springs as physics, in labs/gb/components/shared/spring.ts. readSpring() returns the damping ratio and stiffness of a spring token (Expressive or Standard, whichever applies to the element), and Spring solves it in closed form and samples it every animation frame: Example: A panel driven by a spring with a release velocity HTML CSS TypeScript Under reduced motion the spring jumps to its target and rests at once. DragSettleController (the drag-and-settle behavior behind swipe to reveal, drawers, sheets and pane handles) does this for you when you pass onFrame: the settle starts at the release position with the release velocity, and the surface follows the frames with no CSS transition on the moved property. Without onFrame it keeps the CSS transition of the spring token.

Buttons and icon buttons (md-gb-button, md-gb-icon-button) morph their shape when pressed and when selected. That is spatial motion, so reduced motion turns it off and keeps the color change.

Components that script their motion use the helpers in labs/gb/components/shared/motion.ts: springDuration(element, speed, kind) returns the duration of a spring in milliseconds, already 0 for spatial springs when motion is reduced. isReducedMotion(element) and onReducedMotionChange(...) follow the setting, including inside .md-motion-reduced. waitForMotion(...) resolves when the animations end or when its timeout runs out, so waiting never hangs. waitForDuration(ms, signal) is the plain timed wait.

The spec's Compose APIs (MotionScheme objects, a CompositionLocal per element) have no web equivalent. The CSS steps above replace them. Springs are pre-sampled into linear() easings for transitions. A transition cannot take a starting velocity, so gestures use the solver described in Gestures instead.

M3 Expressive moves components to springs, but transitions still use the easing and duration system, and so can products that have not migrated yet. The spec offers a starting pair for each case: Easing token Duration token Use it to emphasized long2 (500ms) Begin and end on screen emphasized-decelerate medium4 (400ms) Enter the screen emphasized-accelerate short4 (200ms) Exit the screen standard medium2 (300ms) Begin and end on screen, small utility transitions standard-decelerate medium1 (250ms) Enter the screen standard-accelerate short4 (200ms) Exit the screen Example: A sheet that enters with the emphasized decelerate easing HTML CSS JavaScript Tokens are --md-sys-motion-easing-<set>[-accelerate|-decelerate] and --md-sys-motion-duration-<short|medium|long|extra-long><1-4>. Short is 50 to 200ms, medium 250 to 400ms, long 450 to 600ms and extra long 700 to 1000ms, in steps of 50ms (extra long in steps of 100ms). How to choose: Easing set. Emphasized for most transitions, with its decelerate and accelerate variants for entering and exiting. Standard for small, quick, utility transitions. Easing type. Plain for elements that begin and end on screen, decelerate when entering, accelerate when leaving for good. An element that leaves temporarily (a drawer that comes back) uses the plain curve. Duration. Bigger transitions and larger distances take longer. Exits are shorter than enters, because the user's attention has already moved on. Reduced motion does not change these tokens. Gate sliding and scaling yourself (the transition helpers below do) or use the spring tokens, which follow the setting. Not covered: the spec's emphasized easing is a path curve. On the web --md-sys-motion-easing-emphasized is the single cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) approximation, so it is equal to standard.

A transition is a short animation that connects elements or full-screen views and shows how they relate. The spec defines six patterns and notes that they still use the easing and duration tokens above, not springs. labs/gb implements them in styles/motion/transitions/ with the View Transitions API, and falls back to the Web Animations API when the browser lacks it (or when you pass viewTransition: false). The pattern styles are part of m3Styles (see Quick Start). Adopt them on the document, because ::view-transition-* rules only work there. The helpers come from @material/web/labs/gb/styles/motion/transitions/transitions.js. Every helper takes update, a function that changes the DOM to the new state, and returns a promise that resolves when the motion ends. Common options: reducedMotion, viewTransition, duration and easing. The timings come from --md-transition-* custom properties (for example --md-transition-shared-axis-duration), so you can restyle a pattern in CSS.

For an element that becomes a new surface and shows more detail: a card that opens a details page, a FAB that opens a sheet, a search box, a list item. The container's bounds, corner radius and color morph while its content fades through (Emphasized, 500ms by default). from and to can be the same element or different ones. Swap them to collapse back. Example: A card that becomes a details surface and collapses back HTML CSS TypeScript

For screens at consecutive levels of hierarchy, like an inbox and a message. The screens slide along the x axis as they fade (axis: 'y' and 'z' are available too). Always pair forward with backward when the user goes back, so the direction stays consistent. Example: An inbox and a message with forward and backward motion HTML CSS TypeScript scope limits the motion to one region. Without it the whole page animates.

For peers at the same level, like tabs or the photos in an album. Both pages slide the full width together. The direction is next or previous and follows the writing direction (RTL is handled). Example: Two peer pages that slide sideways HTML CSS TypeScript

For switching between top-level destinations (navigation bar, rail or drawer). The old screen quickly fades out, then the new one fades in, so they never overlap. These destinations are not related spatially, so there is no directional slide; the new screen only scales up slightly as it fades in. Example: Switching between top-level destinations HTML CSS TypeScript

For introducing or removing a component. enter(element, options) shows it (hidden = false) and exit(element, options) animates it away, then you hide or remove it. Both resolve when the animation ends. Within screen bounds (menus, dialogs, snackbars, tooltips, FABs). The default style: 'expand' is the Android style: the component expands away from the nearest screen edge, without scale. style: 'scale' is the iOS style (scale in, fade out). Pick the edge with origin. Beyond screen bounds (drawers, sheets, banners, navigation). style: 'slide' slides the component on and off from its edge. Set temporary: true for something that comes back, like a drawer, so it exits with the plain Emphasized curve instead of the accelerate one. Example: A menu that expands downwards and a drawer that slides in HTML CSS TypeScript Match the origin to where the component lives: a notification from the top, a drawer from the start edge, a bottom sheet and the keyboard from the bottom. In templates, enterExitClasses(state, options) returns a classMap() object (md-transition-enter, md-transition-from-top and so on), and clearEnterExit(element) removes the classes. Hide and reveal while scrolling A component can also leave and return based on a scroll gesture, to give more room for browsing: a top app bar or a navigation bar that slides off the screen edge while the user scrolls down and back on when they scroll up. scrollEnterExit(element, options) does this with the slide enter and exit motion and returns a handle with hidden, show(), hide() and destroy(). Example: A top bar that hides while scrolling down HTML CSS TypeScript target is the scrolling element or its id (the window by default), origin the edge it slides toward. It uses the same scroll rules as the app bar and navigation bar, so they all behave alike: it reveals at the top and when scrolled up, hides after a short scroll down, never hides while focus is inside it, and reveals when focus moves into it. A hidden element is inert. With reduced motion it fades instead of sliding. Call destroy() when the element goes away. Components that already have scroll-behavior="hide" do not need this. Coplanar components A coplanar component sits at the same elevation as the main content (a standard side sheet), so the content shrinks to make room as it enters and grows back as it exits. coplanar(element, open, options) animates the element's size from zero to its natural size with the enter motion (and back with the exit motion), so a flex or grid neighbor resizes with it. It shows the element when opening and sets hidden when closing ends. Example: A side panel that makes room for the main content HTML CSS TypeScript axis: 'block' grows the element along the block axis instead of the inline axis. With reduced motion the size changes at once and only a fade plays. md-gb-side-sheet already does this itself: a standard (not modal) sheet takes its width as open is set, so the content beside it shrinks with its spring motion. Use coplanar() for your own panels.

The spec asks transitions to follow accessibility settings, stay consistent, keep layouts stable, avoid jump cuts, use one spatial model and direction, fade cleanly and stay simple. Every helper follows prefers-reduced-motion and replaces sliding and scaling with a quick fade. Pass reducedMotion: true to force it, as an app setting would. Fade through never overlaps the old and new content. The content fade of a container transform is timed to the fastest part of the motion. Use one pattern per kind of navigation, and keep forward and backward mirrored. Dialogs and similar components that appear in place use the short fade (--md-transition-enter-fade-duration).

Keep most of a product on one scheme. Switch schemes only for a few key moments, and do it on purpose. Do not use motion to carry meaning on its own. Reduced motion removes it, so pair it with a change people can see without motion.

pages.d: Time pickers let people choose an hour and minute on a clock dial, or type them into fields.
x: Example: An inline time picker set to 7:00

Dial or input. The dial is quick for picking an approximate time, and typing is faster for an exact one. People can switch between them unless you hide the toggle. Inline or modal. Show the picker inline in a form, or as a modal when it opens from a field or button. Match the locale. The picker follows the 12 or 24 hour clock of its locale. Set hour-cycle to force one.
A time picker has a headline, the hour and minute selectors, an AM or PM toggle in 12 hour mode, a dial, and the actions. Example: A time picker with its headline, selectors, dial and actions

Add modal to show the picker in a dialog with a scrim. Open it with show(). It fires change when a time is confirmed and cancel when it is dismissed. Example: A modal time picker opened from a Set alarm button HTML JavaScript
Set mode="input" to start with hour and minute fields instead of the dial. Add hide-mode-toggle to remove the switch between the two. Example: A time picker with hour and minute fields
Set hour-cycle to 12 or 24. The value is always a 24 hour HH:MM string. Example: A 24 hour time picker set to 20:00

The dial sits below the time selectors (vertical), except in short landscape windows, where it moves beside them (horizontal). Set orientation to choose one. Example: A time picker with a horizontal layout
Set density from 0 (default) to -3 to make the picker more compact. Example: A time picker with a density of -3

Input mode is an alternative to the dial, and every control has a label. Localize the labels with attributes such as select-hour-label, hour-label, cancel-label and confirm-label. pages.d: Spacing is the distance around and between elements.
x: Spacing is the distance around and between elements. It shapes components (the space between an icon and its label) and layouts (the margin between the content and the window edge). Spacing follows an 8dp scale, and tokens keep that scale in one place.

There are three kinds: Padding is the space inside an element, between its edge and its content. Gaps are the spaces between elements in a row, column or grid. Margins are the space outside an element, between it and its parent or the screen edge. Each one can be vertical, horizontal, or on one edge: top, bottom, leading or trailing. Leading and trailing swap sides in right-to-left languages, so write them as logical properties (padding-inline, margin-inline-start). Define padding and gaps on the parent container first. Margins on child elements are harder to keep uniform, so use them only for space beyond the parent's padding, or in a layout.

The unit is --md-sys-space-unit, 8px. Each token is a multiple of it. The token name is the value times 100, so space200 is 2 units (16px). The in-between values (2, 4, 6 and 10px) are nested units for small gaps, such as an icon and its label. pages.d: Install the md-gb elements as React components with the shadcn CLI, themed by your shadcn variables.
x: This site is a shadcn registry at /3.0/r/. npx shadcn@latest add copies a file into your project, adds the npm dependencies, and merges the theme: A React wrapper per component family, such as md-button or md-menu (a menu with its group and item). The file is components/ui/md-<name>.tsx. It registers the md-gb-* elements and wraps each one with @lit/react: typed props from the element class, and the events as onChange, onClose and so on. md-theme, installed with every item: it loads the M3 styles and maps your shadcn variables to the M3 color and shape roles. md-theme-m3, optional: the reverse, the M3 baseline as shadcn variables, so shadcn components match the md-gb elements. The registry lists every item in registry.json.
md-button md-menu onChange onClose md-theme md-theme-m3 registry.json

The plain URL form needs no setup: To use the short form, add the registry to components.json once. The keys of registries start with @, and {name} is the item: The command installs @material/web and @lit/react with your package manager. Each component page has this command after its first example. Use the component like any other. The JSON and TSX blocks on this page are plain blocks and not live demos: the TSX needs React, which this page does not load, and the JSON is configuration with no visible effect.

md-theme adds @import "@material/web/labs/gb/styles/m3.css" to your global CSS, then declares the --md-sys-* variables in :root and in .dark from your shadcn variables. The M3 styles are in a cascade layer and the bridge is not, so the bridge wins regardless of the order of the imports. Change your shadcn theme, or toggle .dark, and the elements follow. It also sets color-scheme for :root and .dark. Containers stay with their on- colors: each pair maps to a pair that shadcn already keeps readable together. The *-fixed roles, scrim and shadow keep the M3 baseline. shadcn has no tertiary role, so it follows primary. outline is the muted foreground and not --border, because M3 needs 3:1 against the surface for the outline of a field or an outlined button; --border is the outline-variant (dividers).
Match shadcn to the M3 baseline

md-theme-m3 goes the other way. It writes the baseline colors of M3 (light and dark) into the shadcn variables: It is independent of md-theme. With both installed, the bridge points the M3 roles at shadcn variables that now hold the M3 colors, so the two agree.

The elements import their styles as CSS module scripts (import styles from './menu.css' with {type: 'css'}). Browsers support that, but Vite, webpack and Node do not without help, and the build fails with "default" is not exported by "…/focus-ring.css". Every stylesheet ships next to a Lit CSSResult module (menu.cssresult.js), so a one-time plugin that points the imports there is enough. For Vite (a plain block; it is configuration with no visible effect):

Tailwind classes style only the host. The elements use shadow DOM, so className="bg-red-500" colors the <md-gb-button> box, not its inside. Customize with the --md-* custom properties and ::part() selectors listed in each component's API reference. They work in a plain CSS file or in Tailwind's arbitrary properties, such as [--container-color:red]. Client only. The wrappers start with 'use client', and the elements cannot be imported in Node (they use CSS module scripts, customElements and document). In Next.js the server renders client components too, so import the file with next/dynamic(() => import('...'), {ssr: false}) or render it after mount, unless you set up Lit SSR. Labs. The elements come from @material/web/labs/gb/. The registry keeps @material/web as the dependency, and the path needs a version that ships labs/gb. Typography, motion and icons are not bridged. Load the Material Symbols font as in the quick start. Local testing. When this site runs from the dev server the registry files point to http://localhost:8000. Set MWC_REGISTRY_URL to build them for another origin. The registry files are generated by scripts/m3/gb-shadcn.mjs from the element sources, so the props and events match the API reference. For agents, the same information is in llms.txt and custom-elements.json.

pages.d: Progress indicators inform people about the status of ongoing processes, such as loading an app or submitting a form.
x: Example: A linear progress indicator at 50 percent and an indeterminate circular one

Pick the variant. Use linear for progress across a page or container and circular for a compact spot such as a button or a card. Use the same style for the same process. Keep one configuration for all the instances of a process, like loading. Show real progress when you know it. Set a value for determinate progress, and leave it off when the length of the process is unknown. Use wavy sparingly. A wavy active indicator is more expressive; use it where that fits your product. For short waits, use a loading indicator. The loading indicator replaces most indeterminate circular progress indicators.
A progress indicator is one element: an active indicator over a track. It is linear unless circular is set. Example: An indeterminate linear progress indicator
The default indicator animates along a horizontal track. Example: An indeterminate and a determinate linear progress indicator
Add circular to animate clockwise along a circular track. Example: An indeterminate and a determinate circular progress indicator
Set value from 0 to 1 when you know how far along the process is. Without a value, the indicator is indeterminate. Example: Linear progress indicators at 25, 50 and 75 percent
Add wavy to give the active indicator a wave. It works on linear and circular indicators, determinate or not. Example: A wavy linear indicator and a wavy circular indicator

A progress indicator is a progressbar. Give it an aria-label that says what is in progress, such as "Download progress". A determinate indicator exposes its value from 0 to 100 to assistive technology. An indeterminate one has no value. Example: A progress indicator labelled Download progress

Refresh content people expect to change. Use it on feeds and lists that update, such as news or messages. Always offer another way. Pulling isn't available to everyone, so provide a refresh button that people can use with a single pointer or the keyboard. Show it is working. Use it in compact and medium windows. From expanded windows up, switch to a navigation rail. Keep three to five destinations. They should be of equal importance. Keep destinations consistent. Set item-layout to vertical (the default) or horizontal. With auto, items are vertical in compact windows and horizontal from 600px. Example: A navigation bar with horizontal items

pages.d: Sheets show supplementary content and actions anchored to the bottom or the side of the window.

Secondary content. Sheets hold extra content and actions, not the main content of the app. Match the window size. Use a bottom sheet in compact and medium windows and a side sheet in wider ones. Standard or modal. A standard sheet sits beside the content so people can keep using it. A modal sheet blocks the page under a scrim until it is closed.
A bottom sheet has a container and an optional drag handle. A side sheet adds a headline, a close button and actions. Example: A bottom sheet and a side sheet, each opened by a button HTML JavaScript

A bottom sheet rests at a partial height and expands when dragged or when its handle is activated. Without modal it is a standard sheet with no scrim. Set state="expanded" to open it at full height. Example: A bottom sheet that opens expanded HTML JavaScript
Add hide-drag-handle to remove the handle and dragging. Add skip-partially-expanded for a sheet that has no partial height. Example: A bottom sheet without a drag handle HTML JavaScript

A side sheet has a headline, a close button and an actions slot. Add divider to separate the actions, and detached to float the sheet with margins. Example: A modal side sheet with Save and Cancel actions HTML JavaScript
Set has-back-button on a side sheet to let people go back to an earlier region. The sheet fires back when it is pressed. Example: A side sheet with a back button HTML JavaScript

A modal sheet is a <dialog>: focus moves into it, stays inside, and returns to the opener on close. Escape and a click on the scrim close it. Name a bottom sheet with label. Keep it about the page. An app bar shows the title, navigation and a few actions that belong to the current page. Limit the actions. Show one action, two if needed, and put many actions in a toolbar. Avoid an overflow menu when you can. Pick a size. Use medium or large for a more expressive headline, and a small bar once content scrolls. Let it respond to scrolling. Set variant="search" and put a text input in the search slot. Example: A search app bar

pages.d: Chips help people enter information, make selections, filter content, or trigger actions.
x: Example: Filter chips in a labeled chip set

Pick the type by purpose. Assist chips are smart actions, filter chips filter content, input chips are information a person entered, and suggestion chips offer dynamic replies or queries. Show chips as a set. Unlike buttons, chips appear dynamically as a group, so always place them in a chip set. Elevate only for protection. Use elevated chips when they sit on an image or a busy background. Keep them compact. Reduce density when space is tight.
A chip set holds chips, and each chip holds its label and optional icons. Example: A chip set with a chip that has a leading and a trailing icon

Assist chips are smart or automated actions, such as adding an event to a calendar. They are the default type, can link with href, and can be elevated. Example: An assist chip with an icon and an assist chip that links to a page

Filter chips use tags or descriptive words to filter content and can replace toggle buttons or checkboxes. Set type="filter" and use selected for chosen ones. Example: Filter chips, one selected, one with a trailing icon

Input chips are discrete pieces of information a person entered, such as contacts. Set type="input"; add removable for a remove button and editable to let people edit the text. Icons and avatars go in the icon slot. Example: Removable input chips, one with an icon
Suggestion chips narrow a person's intent with dynamically generated suggestions, such as possible replies. Example: Suggested replies

The chip set manages selection (selection="single" or "multiple") and arrow-key navigation, and wraps chips by default. With selection="single", add required so the selected chip can't be unselected, or single-line to scroll instead of wrap. Example: A single-select chip set with a heading
Set density on the chip set from 0 (default) to -3 to remove 4px of height per step. Example: A chip set with a density of -2
A soft-disabled chip stays focusable so screen reader users can discover actions that are not available yet, such as Copy before text is selected. Example: A disabled chip and a soft-disabled chip

A chip set is a grid of chips: label it with aria-label or aria-labelledby. Add an aria-label to chips whose text needs to be more descriptive. The set is one tab stop; arrow keys, Home and End move between chips, and Backspace or Delete removes a removable chip. Disabled chips leave the focus order; use soft-disabled where discoverability matters, per the ARIA guidance on disabled controls. pages.d: Dialogs provide important prompts in a user flow.
x: Example: A button that opens a dialog asking to delete messages HTML JavaScript

Use them sparingly. A dialog interrupts people to ask for a decision or to show critical information, so it blocks the rest of the app until it is dismissed. Pick the right priority. For low or medium priority information, use a snackbar instead. Choose basic or full-screen. Use a basic dialog by default. A full-screen dialog suits compact windows with a lot of content. Order the actions. Put the dismissive action first and the confirming action last.

pages.d: Lists are continuous, vertical indexes of text and images, with optional selection, reordering, expanding and swipe actions.
x: Example: A segmented list of three items with supporting and trailing text

Make items easy to scan. Keep labels short, order items in a logical way such as alphabetical or numerical, and show icons, text and actions in a consistent format. Choose a style. A standard list is flat; a segmented list separates each item into its own container. Match the item to its content. Add supporting text, an overline, an avatar or a leading icon to describe what an item is. Add behavior when it helps. Lists can select, reorder, expand and reveal swipe actions.

pages.d: Menus show a temporary set of actions or choices, opened from a button, a text field or a context.
x: Example: A button that opens a menu of file actions

Use it for temporary actions. A menu shows a short set of actions on demand. To show actions on screen at all times, use a toolbar. Open it from many places. A menu can open from a button, an icon button, a split button or a text field, or as a context menu. Organize long menus. Use groups with labels and dividers to separate related choices. Choose a color. The standard color suits most menus; vibrant makes the selected items stand out.

A menu holds items, groups and dividers. An item holds a label and optional slots, including a submenu. Example: A menu with a group, an item with all of its slots, a divider and another item HTML TypeScript

A menu is a popover. Point an md-gb-button (or md-gb-icon-button, or a native button) at it with popovertarget, or call showPopover() from script. The menu positions itself next to the button and closes on Escape, when focus leaves, or when an item is chosen. Example: A button that opens a menu of sort options

Wrap related items in an md-gb-menu-group. Set label for a heading, and checkable to single or multiple to make the items selectable like radio buttons or checkboxes. Use checked on the selected items. Example: A menu with a single-select group and a multi-select group

Set color="vibrant" to use the tertiary color roles instead of the surface-based standard style. Example: A vibrant menu with a checked item
Put an md-gb-menu in an item's submenu slot. It opens beside the item on click, Enter, Space or the Right arrow key (Left in right-to-left layouts). Example: A menu item that opens a submenu
Set context-for to the id of an element to open the menu on a secondary click, the context menu key or a long press. Example: A menu that opens on right-click
Set density from 0 (default) down to -3 to remove 4px of height per item for each step. Submenus inherit it. Keep it off by default and let people opt in. Example: A menu at density -2

The menu has role="menu", and items have role="menuitem", or menuitemradio and menuitemcheckbox in checkable groups. On the button that opens the menu, Up and Down open it and focus the first item; Enter and Space open it natively. In an open menu, Up and Down move between items (disabled items included), Home and End go to the first and last item, and typing a letter jumps to the next item that starts with it. Escape and Tab close the menu and return focus to the button. Left (Right in right-to-left layouts) closes a submenu. Give a menu that has no clear visible title an aria-label.

pages.d: Radio buttons let people select one option from a set of options.
x: Example: A radio group for choosing a delivery address

Use radios for a single choice. Pick radio buttons, not switches, when only one option can be selected from a list; use checkboxes when several can. Show every option. Radios expose all the choices, so use them for five or fewer; consider a menu when space is tight. Always add a label. Each radio needs its own scannable label, and a person can select either the radio or its label. Preselect one and stack them. List radios vertically with one option already selected, and avoid nesting them.
A radio is one element, paired with an adjacent label. Example: A radio button with its label

Radios with the same name form a group, and only one can be selected. Add checked to the one selected at the start, and value to identify the selection in a form. Example: A group of three radios in a form
Add required to any radio in the group to require a selection before the form submits. Example: A required radio group
Add disabled to a radio that can't be selected right now. Example: A radio group with a disabled option
Set density from 0 (default) down to -3 to shrink the radio by 4px per step. The touch target stays 48px. Keep it off by default and let people opt in. Example: A radio group at density -2

Use an aria-label only for a radio with no visible label. Don't wrap a radio in its <label>; screen readers then can't announce the number of radios in the group. Tab moves focus to the selected radio of a group, and the arrow keys move the selection between radios. Space selects the focused radio. Once a radio is selected the group can't be cleared, so add a "None" option or a "Clear selection" control if people may opt out.

pages.d: A search bar lets people enter a query and find matching results, with a search view that shows suggestions and results.
x: Example: A search bar with recipe suggestions

Use it to navigate with queries. Search is the entry point for finding content in a product by typing. Hint what to search. A bar can show hinted text such as "Search recipes", a leading icon and up to two trailing icons. Suggest as people type. The view lists suggestions or results below the bar as the query changes. Choose a style. The contained style is recommended; the divided style puts a divider between the header and the results. Make it prominent. A search app bar gives search an emphasized, global entry point. This component is new in M3 Expressive.

A search bar holds the leading and trailing elements; its default slot holds the suggestions or results shown in its search view. Example: A search bar with leading, trailing and view trailing buttons and suggestions
md-gb-search-bar md-gb-icon-button aria-label md-gb-icon view-trailing md-gb-list-item

Put up to two icon buttons in the trailing slot, or an avatar in the avatar slot. A leading icon button, such as a menu button, replaces the default search icon. Example: A search bar with a menu button and a voice search button
Add docked to open the view as a drop-down below the bar, for medium and larger windows. Without it, the view opens full-screen. Example: A docked search bar
Add divided to use the baseline style, with a divider between the view's header and its results. Example: A search bar with a divided view
Put a search bar in the search slot of an app bar with variant="search". The app bar draws the container, so make the bar's container transparent. Example: A search app bar with a profile button
Use md-gb-search-view on its own for a search that opens from an icon button. Set open from the button. Example: An icon button that opens a search view HTML JavaScript
md-gb-search-view md-gb-icon-button open-search aria-label md-gb-icon md-gb-list-item
Set searching while you wait for results. The view shows a progress indicator and marks the results as busy. Example: A search bar that shows it is searching for a second HTML JavaScript

The bar's input and the view's input are comboboxes, and the suggestions are the options of a listbox. Slotted results without a role get role="option". Enter, the Down arrow or typing opens the view. The back button and Escape close it. The input is named by label, which defaults to placeholder. Set label when the hint isn't a good name. Give icon buttons in the slots an aria-label, such as "Voice search". Change back-label, clear-label, results-label and searching-label when you translate the page. Announce changing results with suggestions-label.

pages.d: Snackbars tell people about a process an app has performed or will perform, without interrupting them.
x: Example: A button that shows a snackbar with an Undo action HTML TypeScript

Low priority only. Use a snackbar for a message that needs no response. For an important one that blocks the task, use a dialog. One at a time. Show a single snackbar, and queue consecutive messages. At most one action. Give it a short action such as Undo. A snackbar with an action stays until it is used or dismissed. Repeat the message nearby. A snackbar that disappears on its own is easy to miss, so also show the result inline, such as changing "Save" to "Saved".

pages.d: A toolbar holds actions that relate to the content on the screen, docked to an edge or floating above it.
x: Example: A floating toolbar with formatting actions

Actions for the page. A toolbar offers actions related to the current page and can show more of them in larger windows. Docked or floating. A docked toolbar spans the window and suits global actions that stay the same across pages. A floating toolbar hovers over the content and suits actions for that content. Vibrant for emphasis. Use the vibrant color for more emphasis. Not with a navigation bar. Don't show a toolbar at the same time as a navigation bar.
A toolbar holds actions, such as buttons and icon buttons. A floating toolbar can have a FAB. Example: A toolbar with leading and trailing buttons, a button and a FAB
md-gb-toolbar aria-label md-gb-icon-button md-gb-icon md-gb-button md-gb-fab
Toolbars are standard by default. Set color="vibrant" for a more prominent toolbar. Example: A vibrant toolbar
Add docked to stretch the toolbar across the full width of its container. Example: A docked toolbar
Toolbars can hold buttons with labels as well as icon buttons. Use toggle buttons to show a selected state. Example: A toolbar with toggle buttons
Set orientation="vertical" to stack the actions in a column. Example: A vertical toolbar

A floating toolbar can sit beside a FAB in the fab slot. Set fab-position="start" to move it to the leading side, or expanded="false" to collapse the toolbar to just the FAB. Example: A floating toolbar with a FAB
Add overflow-menu to move trailing actions that don't fit into a "More actions" menu. Example: A narrow toolbar with an overflow menu
overflow-menu md-gb-toolbar aria-label max-inline-size md-gb-icon-button md-gb-icon

Set scroll-behavior="hide" to move a docked or floating toolbar off screen when the page scrolls down and bring it back when it scrolls up. scroll-target names the element that scrolls; it defaults to the window. Example: A docked toolbar that hides when its page scrolls down HTML CSS
scroll-target md-gb-toolbar scroll-behavior aria-label md-gb-icon-button md-gb-icon block-size overflow-y padding-inline inset-block-end margin-block

A toolbar has the toolbar role. Label it with aria-label or aria-labelledby. Every action stays in the Tab order, and the arrow keys also move between them (up and down in a vertical toolbar). Icon-only actions need an aria-label. A collapsed toolbar makes its hidden actions inert.

pages.d: Tooltips add context to a button or other element, as a short plain label or a richer panel with a subhead and actions.
x: Example: A plain tooltip on an icon button

Plain to label. Use a plain tooltip to name an element with no text, such as an icon-only button. Don't add one when the element already has a visible label. Rich for details. Use a rich tooltip for longer text, such as a definition or an explanation of a new feature, with an optional subhead and up to two text buttons. Nothing critical. Tooltips are easy to miss, so never hide information people must see. Use a dialog for that.
A tooltip points at an anchor element by its id. A rich tooltip can add a subhead and actions. Example: A rich tooltip with a subhead, text and an action, open on a button HTML JavaScript

A plain tooltip opens above its anchor and a rich one below it. Set placement to above, below, start or end; it flips when there isn't room. Add caret to point at the anchor. Example: A plain tooltip with a caret, placed below its anchor
Set variant="rich" and a subhead. Text buttons go in the action slot. Example: A rich tooltip with a subhead and an action
A persistent rich tooltip opens when the anchor is clicked and stays open until someone interacts with something else, so people can reach its actions. Example: A rich tooltip that opens on click

A tooltip opens right away and closes 1.5 seconds after the pointer leaves. Set show-delay and hide-delay in milliseconds, or add quick to skip the motion. Example: A tooltip that closes after half a second
show-delay hide-delay md-gb-icon-button aria-label md-gb-icon md-gb-tooltip

A plain tooltip is a tooltip that describes its anchor, and it opens on hover and on keyboard focus. Keep the anchor's own accessible name, such as an aria-label on an icon button. A rich tooltip with actions is a dialog, so its buttons can be reached with the keyboard. Escape closes an open tooltip. Don't put information in a tooltip that people can't find another way, since touch users can't hover.
